系统采用 Rust/Axum、Next.js、PostgreSQL/pgvector 和 DeepSeek。已审核笔记用于图谱更新，计划预期知识独立保存并与实际记录匹配；已审核资料经分块和向量化参与项目内混合检索。固定任务按模板读取证据，会话工具按项目权限过滤，高风险操作经人工确认，重复请求受幂等控制，来源与工具调用写入审计记录。

before.text: University research groups retain experimental objectives, conditions, materials, procedures, and results for collaboration, traceability, and reuse. Paper notebooks and scattered files hinder record checking, version management, handovers, and structured use of experimental entities. This thesis designs and implements an electronic laboratory notebook (ELN) with unified records, project permissions, review workflows, and verifiable sources.
Requirements analysis identified needs for full-lifecycle note management, project-level permission isolation, reviewed knowledge ingestion, verifiable answer sources, and controlled AI assistance.

This thesis develops three engineering innovations: (1) review-driven knowledge updates and plan-coverage checking, which store planned knowledge separately from reviewed records and match the two; (2) joint retrieval of document passages and direct experimental-object relations with source verification; and (3) AI assistance constrained by project permissions, human confirmation, and idempotency, which prevents repeated requests from producing duplicate writes.

Built with Rust/Axum, Next.js, PostgreSQL/pgvector, and DeepSeek, the system updates graphs on note approval and matches separately stored planned knowledge points against reviewed records. Reviewed documents support project-scoped hybrid retrieval through chunking and vectorization. Source identifiers and a graph interface link retrieved passages and direct relations to their origins. Fixed tasks use reviewed evidence and templates; permission-filtered session tools enforce high-risk confirmation, idempotency, and audit logging.

Archived records show that eight browser end-to-end scenarios and eight tests of high-risk confirmation and idempotency passed. Relation extraction from four synthetic seed notes matched 52 author-defined reference relations in a string-set comparison. In the historical Python prototype, ordinary retrieval-augmented generation and graph-enhanced generation completed 4/20 and 14/20 questions under the rule-based measure. A unified offline check of citation-marker syntax and array bounds passed 17/20 and 15/20 archived answers, respectively. Supplementary GPT semantic review, question-answer retesting with rules set before generation, and role-based API verification further assessed answer evidence and business operations.

Scanned records can enter the project knowledge base after optical character recognition and manual correction. It also supports graph and source browsing, project question answering and evaluation, fixed-task generation, plan-coverage checking, on-demand alerts, and audit queries.

This thesis develops three engineering innovations: (1) review-driven knowledge updates and plan-coverage checking, which store planned knowledge separately from reviewed records and match the two; (2) joint retrieval of document passages and direct experimental-object relations with source verification; and (3) AI assistance constrained by project permissions, human confirmation, and idempotency, which reuses results for the same user, tool, idempotency key, and parameters.

Built with Rust/Axum, Next.js, PostgreSQL/pgvector, and DeepSeek, the system updates graphs on note approval and compares planned knowledge points with reviewed records. Reviewed documents undergo chunking and vectorization for project-scoped hybrid retrieval. Source identifiers link document passages and direct relations to their origins. Fixed tasks use reviewed evidence and templates; session tools enforce permissions, high-risk confirmation, idempotency, and audit logging.

Archived records show that eight browser end-to-end scenarios and eight high-risk confirmation and idempotency tests passed. Extraction from four synthetic seed notes achieved 100.00% precision, recall, and F1 against 52 internally compiled reference relations; these scores describe agreement with that checklist. In 20 archived questions from the Python prototype before its migration to Rust, ordinary retrieval and graph-enhanced retrieval completed 4/20 and 14/20 questions under the rule-based measure, while citation syntax and range checks passed 17/20 and 15/20 answers.
